Recorded study · continuity, crossing and depth

Following a strand through a weave

A strand can disappear under another and still remain connected. This experiment keeps its route, its local crossing order and its visible ribbon available as separate reads of the same structure.

Start with the black ribbon, then reveal the colored strands or the small depth samples. Compare controlled changes to see which facts survive. The continuation examples below ask a second question—what can visible fragments justify when the hidden route has not been supplied?

Explore the weaveCompare readingsHidden continuationsStudy notes
This is an authored reconstruction inspired by the supplied angular ornament. The selected connections and crossing orders are explicit premises. The image alone does not establish its original machine, strand count or hidden route. Ribbon thickness and the displayed height are illustrative.
1. Keep the route

A hidden section retains its actual endpoints and place in the strand. An absent section leaves a different result.

2. Read each encounter

Front and back belong to a local crossing. A strand can be above here and below at its next encounter.

3. Preserve alternatives

Aligned fragments can support a continuation candidate. Shared identity and a witnessed return route provide stronger evidence.

Explore the weave

Change one structural condition at a time. Select a crossing to inspect the actual section references and its depth order.

View

The visible black ribbon. Local undercuts hide a small part of the lower strand while its native route stays connected.

What connects to what in the construction
  • Four ordered section scopes retain independent endpoint identities.
  • A two-phase exchange controller selects identity or reflected common-reach words for each bay.
  • Substitution and additive placement receipts retain each generated section and the reusable local word it consumed.
  • Each crossing references two actual sections and a projected position word; it creates no shared endpoint.
  • A local order references the actual front and back section, followed by a local two-ended depth relation.
  • Material selection refers to actual sections. Occlusion leaves this selection intact.
  • Encounter predictions retain their strand, crossing, phase and finite-law exchange result. Observed order may disagree or stay open.

Crossing or junction?

The same projected X can describe two passing routes or four arms meeting at one actual site. The shared site changes what a routing law could do. These controls leave depth order open.

Following a strand through a weave

This experiment asks what a small interlaced ornament needs beyond an ordinary repeating path. Follow each coloured strand, then look at the same structure as black ribbon. A strand can disappear underneath another while its route remains continuous. The crossing specifies which strand is in front at that encounter. It does not join the two strands.

The second question starts with less information. If only two visible pieces remain, does their alignment support a hidden connection? The experiment keeps a proposed continuation separate from a known connection. Even a convincing proposal leaves its missing connection open until further evidence or an explicit construction supplies it.

The source is the angular interlaced band supplied in the conversation. This is an authored, idealized reconstruction and a collection of controlled changes. It does not identify the original maker's construction or automatically trace the supplied image. The renderer chooses the displayed size, ribbon width, clearance and depth exaggeration.

Three things to keep separate

Question Structural evidence What it leaves open
Where does this strand continue? Ordered sections whose successive ends share a site Whether the strand is visible throughout
Which strand is in front here? A crossing tied to the two actual sections, with a local front/back relation The height elsewhere and the history of making the weave
Could these fragments connect? Exposed positions, endpoint directions, a selected occluder and candidate relations Whether the hidden connection actually exists

Coordinate equality alone supplies none of these connections. Two sections can cross in a drawing while remaining independent. Two ends can occupy the same display position while retaining different site identities.

A very small depth read

At a resolved crossing, the front strand can be displayed at +h and the back strand at -h. The amount h is a presentation choice. The important information is their local order. One strand may be above at one crossing and below at the next, so assigning one global layer to each strand would lose the weave.

The view exposes the ordered depth samples along each strand. Connecting those samples visually illustrates a possible shallow lift. It does not assert a measured height, a physical bend law, an exact three-dimensional ribbon or a collision-free embedding. Unknown crossing order remains unknown.

An over/under alternation is a relation between successive encounters along a route. It is different from alternating by screen position or by the order in which a drawing program happened to discover crossings. Reversing traversal reverses the encounter sequence. Exchanging front and back changes the depth read. Reflecting the planar geometry is a third operation.

Reading several symmetries

A useful signature retains several questions instead of collapsing them into one score.

  • Does the projected route geometry correspond?
  • Are the same native connections preserved?
  • Does the correspondence preserve each strand or exchange strands?
  • Does it preserve the local over/under order?
  • Does it require reversing depth as well as transforming the plane?
  • Do successive crossing visits retain their alternating rhythm?

Changing one local crossing can leave all projected centerlines unchanged. Removing a section changes participation and continuity. Replacing a crossing with a shared junction changes possible routes. These changes should have different signatures even where a small drawing makes them look similar.

The first recorded results

The baseline contains four separate strands across three repeated bays. Its 42 sections produce 24 projected crossings. Following the crossing visits in each strand's actual order gives 44 adjacent encounter pairs, all alternating. No strand closes within this finite view. The eight ends belong to the four continuing routes at the boundary of the selected drawing.

Controlled change Material components / ends Known material crossing orders Alternating adjacent encounters
Baseline 4 / 8 24 / 24 44 / 44
Reverse one crossing 4 / 8 24 / 24 41 / 44
Reverse every depth order 4 / 8 24 / 24 44 / 44
Reflect the planar construction 4 / 8 24 / 24 44 / 44
Omit one material section 5 / 10 24 / 24 44 / 44
Leave one crossing order unknown 4 / 8 23 / 24 41 / 41
Shift one inner strand 4 / 8 24 / 24 44 / 44
Omit a section through two crossings 5 / 10 22 / 22 38 / 38

The omitted section lies between encounters. The over/under rhythm survives while the material continuity fails. This shows why a rhythm signature alone cannot account for the object.

An unknown crossing leaves three neighbouring comparisons unscored in this finite sample. The reader does not jump over the unknown encounter and compare its former neighbours as though they were adjacent. A result of 41 out of 41 therefore carries less coverage than the baseline's 44 out of 44.

The selected inner-strand displacement also preserves the over/under rhythm. Its positions have changed, but this particular reading is insensitive to that change. A later clearance or spacing reader may distinguish it. This study does not assign a quality penalty merely because the parameter was changed.

A second omission removes a section that actually passes through two crossing sites. Those encounters remain in the construction record, but they no longer supply material over/under readings. The view distinguishes this from hiding an intact section behind another strand.

The bounded repeat comparison tests the proposed strand correspondence [1, 0, 3, 2] after one bay and [0, 1, 2, 3] after two. These are labels for the four actual route scopes in this read. The shorter repeat exchanges the two outer roles and the two inner roles. The longer repeat preserves each named role. Neither translation returns a strand to the same physical endpoint, so neither proves closure. The checks cover the available overlapping part of the three-bay sample. The mappings and candidate periods are supplied by this experiment. The reader checks their segment and crossing correspondences; it does not search all possible periods or strand permutations.

The phase mechanisms are supplied constructions. A two-state exchange law selects the reflected or unreflected profile for successive bays. Independent encounter sequences use a two-state exchange law to offer their local over/under roles. The recorded orders can disagree with those offers or remain open. This is a small executable law over structure, with authored inputs and geometry; it is not a learned generator or a simulation of moving physical ribbon.

What the structural encoding contains

The native root connects the common frame and reach, a repeat displacement, the phase controller, four ordered strand scopes, local crossings and the generation witnesses. Each strand connects its full construction route to a selection of actual material sections. A material omission edits that selection. An occlusion changes the visible read while leaving the selection intact.

In simplified notation, the central relationships are:

strand       -> ordered sections -> shared endpoint handoffs
material     -> selected actual sections
crossing     -> (actual section A, actual section B, projected location)
local order  -> (that crossing, front section, back section)
depth sample -> (actual section, end of this crossing's depth relation)
phase step   -> (current phase, exchange law read, next phase)

The table identifiers on the page are read addresses for inspection. They do not create the connections. No universal participation, uncertainty or depth bit has been added to the historical ODV word. This pass composes the existing qualitative relation grammar and executes its finite laws.

The separate X comparison holds projected support constant while changing native incidence. Two full crossing sections form two components. Four arms sharing one central site form one component with a four-way junction. The junction supplies possible connectivity; a switch or material transfer law would be an additional connected construction.

From alignment to possible closure

The continuation reader receives only selected exposed fragment surfaces and the occluder premise. It does not consult a concealed original path to decide the answer. Collinearity, compatible directed tangents and coverage of the missing interval can support a candidate. Another candidate can pass the same local checks. Without the occluder premise, an ordinary gap stays a gap under this particular reader.

These are independent small fixtures for the continuation rule. Their opaque rectangle is supplied as an observation premise. This pass does not extract those fragment ports or discover the occluding object from the photograph.

Tangent compatibility is weaker than knowing the hidden curve. Many different curves can meet the same endpoint directions. This pass preserves that freedom instead of manufacturing an interpolation and calling it recovered evidence. For curved candidates, the rectangular occluder test covers the endpoint chord. It does not certify that every possible connecting curve stays behind that rectangle.

If the exposed remainder already supplies a return route, a candidate bridge can describe conditional closure. That means the route would close if the candidate were connected. Actual closure requires the appropriate endpoint identities and connections throughout the cycle. Repetition into the next motif also remains different from returning to the same physical site.

What is implemented and what remains open

The construction uses the existing qualitative motion frame, curve sections, crossing reads and ordered relations. Native structure carries the connections. The page's names, colours, table identifiers and numerical coordinates are diagnostic or presentation reads.

This is a bounded, authored experiment. It does not learn the supplied pattern, recover an unknown number of strands from pixels, solve general knot topology, or discover every hidden continuation. The earlier cardinal-course whitespace reader is not applied to diagonal ribbon gaps. A later gap reader must preserve the distinction between projected white space, an occlusion break and physical space between ribbons.

The useful next learning problem is to compare competing connected explanations of the same fragments, retain their different consequences, and test them on new observations. A good local continuation cue can help with that without being promoted to a proof of the entire object.

Reproduce the recorded study

From the repository root:

dotnet run --project experiments/QualitativeFrieze -c Release -- --angular-weave --output artifacts/angular-weave
python experiments/QualitativeFrieze/Composition/AngularWeavePage.py artifacts/angular-weave/study-data.json Visualizations/Gojo.Demos.Web/ornaments/weave
node Visualizations/Gojo.Demos.Web/tools/build-ornaments.mjs

The C# experiment records native structural reads. The page adapter presents those recorded results and converts this Markdown document to HTML. The website is published at https://gojo.inklingai.ca/ornaments/weave/.

Gojo ornament studies. The diagrams are presentation reads of the recorded experiment. Construction, observation, candidate completion and actual topology retain their separate evidence.
